newsitem.title: IRAQ: Saddam hits at Iran over POWs and planes.
newsitem.headline: Saddam hits at Iran over POWs and planes.

text.p: President Saddam Hussein on Friday marked the anniversary of the end of the 1980-1988 Iraq-Iran war by demanding Iran's new president frees Iraqi prisoners of war.

In a speech carried live by Iraqi radio and television, Saddam said it was against the principles of Islam to "murder and mutilate bodies of (Iraqi) prisoners of war after each battle (with Iran) and to keep in captivity others for 17 years...."
Iran denies it still holds Iraqi POWs.
Saddam urged new Iranian President Mohammad Khatami to fulfill Iran's commitments toward Iraq by releasing Iraqi prisoners from the war.
Saddam said Iraq had freed all 39,000 Iranian POWs except for a pilot whose plane was downed during the early days of the war and who was being held to prove that Iran started the war.
According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, more than 13,000 Iraqi POWs have not been repatriated. Iraq says the number exceeds 20,000.

Saddam demanded that Tehran also return civil and military aircraft which flew to Iran at the start of the 1991 Gulf War to escape bombing by the U.S.-led multinational force that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait.
He told the rulers of Iran to abandon their "policy of expansion, illegitimate ambitions...and to adopt instead a policy of cooperation...to stablise and develop (bilateral) relations."
"Other than that we will still not be content to see Iran merely changing posts and replacing an individual or a party with another," Saddam said in the 90-minute speech.
The Iraqi leader reiterated previous Iraqi accusation that Iran was to blame for the instability in Iraq's south which started soon after the ceasefire of the 1991 Gulf War.
"At that time they (Iranians) pushed the most evil people...to burn and to destroy everything that was not reached by bombs of the 30-state aggression," Saddam said.
He said the Iranian rulers tried to push Iraq into an earlier confrontation with the U.S.-led allies in 1991 in order not to "lose the opportunity of betrayal."
"They used to tell our visiting comrades at the time that Iraq would come out victorious if it was the first to attack the allies' armies (U.S. allies against Iraq)," he said.
Saddam charged that after the start of the Iraq-Iran war, Tehran had snubbed 215 peace calls from Iraq and Islamic states.
